note: The twenty-one readings are a contract, and `evals/assertions/tokenise-readings.test.js` proves the mechanics of reading them: which keyword means which reading, which value survives a round trip, which CSS a declaration becomes. None of that is what this eval grades. This grades the half a contract table cannot hold — the shape of the conversation that gathers the eighteen optional readings, which is judgement rather than pass-or-fail. Two behaviours, and both of them rot silently. First, the follow-up: eighteen readings must be gathered in exactly ONE question, asked after the three core readings are settled, and a skipped follow-up must record nothing at all rather than a helpful default. A second question is a form, and a default is an invention. Second, the conflict questions: `superscript` with `subscript` contradicts, `font-variant` over `small-caps` or over `slashed-or-lining-zero` overlaps, and three numbers already named with different optional readings is a near-duplicate. Every one of those must warn and ask — never refuse, never auto-resolve, never silently drop — and the answer is the only thing that ever removes a reading. `underline` with `strikethrough` is the deliberate counter-case: it shares one declaration rather than colliding, so it must NOT become a question. A release that turned that pair into a question would still pass every assertion in the suite. Nothing here calls a model: `parseProse`, `readingsQuestion`, `followUpReadings`, `conflictQuestions`, `settleConflict`, `nearDuplicate` and `declarationTextFor` are the real functions in the real order, walked without a terminal, so every case is reproducible on any machine.
